html:
Full Tear-Off and Replacement for Winston-Salem Roofs

Tear-off and replacement is the right call when a roof has failed past the point recovery can fix — saturated insulation, a deck that's lost structural integrity, or a layer count that already exceeds what code allows to remain in place. We run this as a documented process from demolition through final inspection, because a replacement roof is the one capital project an owner expects to not think about again for two decades. The replacement plan explains tear-off or recover assumptions, insulation and drainage needs, occupied-building phasing, system options, and closeout requirements.

When Tear-Off Is the Only Defensible Option

Some conditions leave no room for a recover decision. Wet insulation that's lost R-value and can't dry from below. A steel deck with active corrosion. A membrane system that's already had one recover layer added, putting it at the code-permitted maximum. Older manufacturing buildings around Thomasville and Lexington, and some of the legacy furniture-industry warehouse stock near High Point, often carry this history — a roof that's been patched and recovered more than once with no records kept. In those cases we document deck condition with photos and moisture readings before demolition starts, so the owner has a record of why full replacement was necessary, backed by evidence rather than a bare invoice.

Demolition Sequencing and Deck Protection

Tear-off exposes the building interior to weather the moment the old membrane comes up, so sequencing matters more here than on any other service we perform. We section the roof into daily tear-off zones sized to what the crew can install new insulation, cover board, and membrane over before end of day. Temporary night seals go down over any zone that can't be fully dried in — this is standard practice, not a contingency plan, because Piedmont summer thunderstorms build fast and without much warning in the afternoon.

  • Existing membrane, insulation, and cover board removed down to deck
  • Deck inspected and repaired or replaced where corrosion or rot is found
  • New insulation installed to current code R-value requirements
  • Cover board and membrane installed per manufacturer fastening spec
  • Edge metal, flashing, and penetrations detailed to manufacturer standard
  • Final walk-through and moisture scan before crew demobilizes

Deck Repair and Structural Findings

Once the old system is off, the deck tells the truth about what's been happening underneath it. Steel deck with rust-through, wood deck with rot at the perimeter, or gypsum deck that's absorbed moisture over years — these show up during tear-off even when a pre-project inspection missed them because the membrane was masking the damage. We stop and document any structural finding before proceeding, get it in front of the owner or their structural engineer if the scope changes, and get sign-off before installing new roofing over a deck that hasn't been properly repaired.

Code Compliance on New Construction

A full replacement is treated as new construction for code purposes, which means current energy code insulation requirements apply even if the building is decades old. We calculate the required R-value for the roof assembly under the North Carolina energy code and specify insulation thickness accordingly — this is often a meaningful upgrade from what came off the building, especially on older manufacturing and warehouse stock built before current energy standards. Wind uplift design also gets recalculated for the building's actual exposure category rather than assumed from the old system's performance.

Scheduling Around Weather and Operations

Full tear-off carries more weather exposure risk than any other roofing service, so we watch the forecast closely and adjust daily tear-off zone size when thunderstorm risk is elevated, which in this region runs heaviest from late spring through early fall. For occupied buildings — schools, medical offices, active manufacturing floors — we coordinate the demolition schedule to avoid the highest-risk weather windows over sensitive interior spaces and keep emergency dry-in materials staged on site for the duration of the project.

Closeout Documentation

At project completion, the owner receives a closeout package: as-built roof assembly details, manufacturer warranty registration, deck repair records if applicable, and inspection sign-offs from the local jurisdiction. This paperwork matters for insurance renewals, for a future sale of the property, and for whoever manages the roof's next maintenance cycle.

Coordinating Trades on a Full Replacement

A tear-off and replacement often touches other trades before it's finished — rooftop mechanical units may need to be temporarily disconnected and reset on new curbs, electrical conduit runs across the roof deck may need rerouting, and fall protection anchor points typically need reinstallation once the new membrane is down. We sequence these handoffs with the general contractor or facilities team so mechanical downtime is scheduled rather than improvised mid-project. On manufacturing buildings with rooftop process equipment, this coordination often determines whether the project stays on schedule, since equipment access windows are usually tighter than the roofing work itself.

Material Staging and Site Logistics

Full tear-off and replacement moves a large volume of material on and off a site — old membrane and insulation coming down, new insulation, cover board, and membrane rolls going up. We plan crane placement, dumpster location, and material staging around the building's existing traffic patterns, particularly for distribution and manufacturing sites where blocking a dock door or access lane for even part of a day has a real cost. For downtown sites with limited lay-down space, staging gets planned around available curb access and any permitting the city requires for lane or sidewalk closures during the project.

Questions Owners Ask Before a Full Replacement

How do you decide between recover and full tear-off?

Deck moisture, existing layer count against code limits, and structural condition drive the decision. If the deck can't be verified sound or the roof is already at its recover limit, tear-off is the only compliant path.

What happens if you find deck damage after tear-off starts?

We stop, document the finding with photos, and bring it to the owner before proceeding. Any scope change for deck repair is priced and approved before new roofing goes down over it.

How long does a full tear-off and replacement take?

It depends on roof size and deck condition, but we section the work into daily zones sized to what can be fully dried in each day, which keeps the building protected throughout rather than leaving it exposed overnight.

Does a tear-off trigger new energy code requirements?

Yes. Full replacement is treated as new construction for insulation R-value purposes, so older buildings typically see an insulation upgrade as part of the project.

What documentation do we get at the end of the project?

A closeout package covering as-built assembly details, manufacturer warranty registration, any deck repair records, and inspection approvals from the local building department.
